Root field yields the raw event payload value

blocks.title: Topic + Projection
items: Root field = topic name plus filter args
Selection set = projection applied to each event
One operation maps to one event source

blocks.title: Not incremental delivery
blocks.text: `@defer` and `@stream` chunk ONE operation's response. A subscription is an open-ended feed of separate results.
The GraphQL spec defines execution only. How bytes reach the client is a protocol you layer on top.

items: WebSocket: `Upgrade: websocket`, 101, full duplex TCP
New subscribes ride the same socket, no reconnect
SSE: `text/event-stream`, one-way, `Last-Event-ID` resume
EventSource auto-reconnects in the browser for free
Long poll: hold request until event or timeout, reissue
Long poll is simplest to deploy, worst per-event overhead
gzip over a whole SSE stream beats per-frame deflate

SSE inherits connection multiplexing from HTTP/2
The '6 connections per origin' limit largely disappears
That was a core WebSocket argument; it has weakened
SSE heartbeat: a `:` comment line on an interval
WebSocket heartbeat: Ping / Pong control frames
Load balancers silently drop idle sockets, typically 60s
Heartbeat interval must sit under that idle timeout

slides.page_title: Transport: WebSocket vs SSE vs Long Poll

blocks.title: Practical default
items: Read-only clients: SSE, every time
Escalate to WebSocket for real multiplexing
Long poll only under legacy constraints

blocks.title: Serverless caveat
blocks.text: No single process owns the socket across invocations, so WebSocket needs a connection registry — API Gateway connection IDs or equivalent.

items: `graphql-ws` speaks the `graphql-transport-ws` subprotocol
That is the modern standard, start here

Read the subprotocol on the wire, not the package name

blocks.title: Subprotocol mismatch
blocks.text: Negotiation happens in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A name mismatch between client and server is the number one cause of a silently dead connection.

items: Every `Subscribe` carries a client-chosen `id`
`Next`, `Error`, `Complete` echo that id back
That echo is how one socket multiplexes many streams
`Error` terminates that id; `Complete` is the clean end
Client sends `Complete` to unsubscribe
Distinct connections mode: one stream per operation, stateless
Stateless means CDN and proxy friendly
Single connection mode: reservation stream plus separate POSTs
`event:` is `next` or `complete`, result JSON in `data:`

blocks.title: Two more facts
items: Queries and mutations can ride these protocols
graphql-ws runs them as one `Next` plus `Complete`
Keep them on plain HTTP so caching still works
Ping/Pong here is app level, survives frame-stripping layers
`subscribe` returns an AsyncIterable of raw events
`resolve` maps each raw event to the field value
With no `resolve`, payload must be keyed by field name
Wrong key yields `null` with no error at all
`next()` yields events, `return()` runs on unsubscribe
Release broker subscriptions and timers inside `return()`
Skip it and a dead client holds a Redis channel forever
Memory then grows monotonically until the pod dies
Context is built once from the `ConnectionInit` payload
Not per event, so it holds auth that ages badly
Never carry a request-scoped DataLoader into a stream

blocks.title: Backpressure
blocks.text: An AsyncIterable that ignores consumer speed buffers without bound. Cap the queue, then drop events or disconnect the slow consumer.

blocks.q: Why do updates work locally but only sometimes in prod?
a_bullets: N pods behind a load balancer, no shared broker
Mutation lands on pod A, subscriber sits on pod B
Delivery succeeds roughly 1/N of the time
Looks like flakiness; it is architecture

items: `graphql-redis-subscriptions`: fire and forget fan-out
At-most-once, no persistence, no replay
Event published during a reconnect is lost forever
Needs TWO clients: subscriber mode blocks other commands
Redis Streams adds replay from an ID plus consumer groups
Durable partitioned log, ordering held per partition
Right when events are also a system of record

blocks.text: Debezium or logical replication turns table writes into events, so a forgotten `publish` call can never make subscriptions drift from the database.

items: Missed event = stale UI until refresh? Redis is fine

For fat payloads, re-check rights at delivery time
Browsers cannot set headers on a WebSocket handshake
So no `Authorization: Bearer` on the upgrade

Never in the URL query string: proxy logs, access logs, history

blocks.title: Denial of wallet
blocks.text: Thousands of cheap subscriptions to one high-volume topic turn your fan-out into your invoice. Cap subscriptions before an attacker finds the ceiling.

items: One publish times N subscribers = N executions
Plus N serializations of the same shape
CPU grows with subscriber count, not with write rate
Budget roughly tens of KB per open subscription
File descriptor limits (`ulimit -n`) bite first
Ephemeral port exhaustion on the proxy tier bites second
Application CPU is rarely the ceiling you hit
Raise LB idle timeout above your heartbeat interval
Never terminate connections on a routine config reload
Every rolling deploy disconnects 100% of subscribers
They all reconnect at once: a self-inflicted thundering herd
Cure: jittered exponential backoff plus a drain window
Split the socket gateway from the query API
Socket load then cannot starve request latency
Sticky sessions unneeded if the broker reaches every node
Each node subscribes and pushes to the sockets it holds
Autoscale on connection count, not CPU; scale in after draining
Dedupe identical documents on the same topic
10,000 clients, one execution, one serialized broadcast
Live queries push diffs instead: simpler client, heavy server
Federated subscriptions resolve in one subgraph, router proxies
You cannot fan one subscription across subgraphs

blocks.title: Bandwidth math
blocks.text: 50k subscribers times 1 event/sec times 2KB is about 100 MB/s of egress. Bandwidth, not compute, is usually the binding constraint.

caption.text: Most teams reach for GraphQL subscriptions and inherit a broker, a reconnect state machine, and a cache reconciliation problem — to save 2.5 seconds nobody asked for. This handbook walks the whole stack: the two-phase execution model, graphql-transport-ws message by message, pub/sub backends from EventEmitter to Kafka, fan-out cost math, and the exact arithmetic that tells you to just poll instead. Ten pages, every gotcha we have paid for.
